paragraphs.text: A [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from Guangxi, made in 1990 and sold as loose leaf. At thirty-six years it sits far past the decade after which the trade counts this tea as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged), and how it was stored has shaped it as much as the years have.

Liu Bao is the [dark tea](dark:definition) of Cangwu County, near Wuzhou, named for the town of Liubao where it began. As with every post-fermented tea, the leaf is piled after it is made, so warmth, moisture and microbes slowly turn it darker before it is packed and left to age. It was made for a market far from home: Chinese miners and labourers in the [tin mines of Malaya](liu-bao:nanyang-trade) drank it, and it travelled by boat down the river to Wuzhou, on to Guangzhou, and out by sea.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
